title: AgentXRay: White-Boxing Agentic Systems via Workflow Reconstruction
one_liner: Recover an editable workflow for a black-box agent by searching for a small chain of roles and tool calls that matches its input-output behavior.
lead: Many deployed agent systems are hard to inspect. A user can send a task and see the answer, but cannot see which roles were used, which tool calls were made, or where waste entered the process. AgentXRay reconstructs a stand-in workflow from input-output examples so that people can inspect and edit a readable version of the system because workflow structure matters for control and debugging.

problem.h2: Why black-box agents are hard to control
paras: A black-box agent can solve a task while hiding the process that produced the answer. That makes it hard to tell whether the system is using too many steps, relying on the wrong tool, or mixing several roles in a wasteful order because the user never sees the intermediate decisions.

Input-output testing alone is limited because two systems can give similar answers while using very different internal workflows. If you want a system that you can edit, audit, or simplify, you need a readable stand-in process rather than only a score on final outputs.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Search over candidate role-and-tool workflows until one reproduces the black-box outputs closely enough to serve as an editable stand-in.

steps.text: List the possible roles, tool calls, and chain positions that a candidate workflow may use.

steps.b: Run the candidate workflow on observed inputs
steps.text: Execute the current stand-in workflow so that its outputs can be compared with the black-box outputs.
Measure how close the candidate outputs are to the target outputs because the stand-in only matters if it reproduces the visible behavior.
Use tree search to add new roles or tool calls where the current partial workflow still looks promising.
Remove candidates that are too weak for their depth so that more of the search budget goes to plausible workflows.

paras: The paper changes the goal from predicting outputs directly to reconstructing a workflow that produces those outputs. That shift matters because the result is a process a user can inspect and alter.
object.object: the explicit workflow that stands in for a hidden agent

hidden.name: which workflow best explains the black-box behavior
paras: The central hidden quantity is the workflow that best explains the black-box system's behavior. You cannot observe that workflow directly, and the real system may not even have a tidy named workflow inside it.

AgentXRay treats workflow choice as a hidden explanation problem. It searches for the smallest chain of roles and tools that reproduces the target outputs well enough because a compact readable workflow is easier to inspect and change.

heat.caption: The search gives the most weight to choices that strongly affect output similarity and search cost.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is the readable process that best matches what the black-box system seems to do.
The method reconstructs a chain-structured workflow by searching over discrete role and tool decisions under an output-based proxy score.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: search for process, not only answers
paras: A single correct answer does not reveal how it was produced. AgentXRay therefore searches over workflows and scores each one against visible outputs. Over many examples, weak workflows fall behind because they cannot keep matching the target behavior across different inputs.

The pruning rule matters because the workflow space grows quickly with depth. If the search keeps every partial branch, most of the budget is wasted on branches that already look poor. By combining quality and depth in the pruning score, the method spends more trials on branches that still have a realistic path to a good stand-in workflow.

stages.s: Prune weak branches by quality and depth

math.h2: Score a workflow by output match minus search cost
math.words: A compact view is to reward workflows that imitate the black-box outputs and penalize depth or wasted complexity. The search then keeps workflows with higher total value.

items.b: The proxy score may miss hidden differences.
items.html: Two workflows may give similar outputs on the test set even though they would behave differently on new tasks, because the visible proxy cannot capture every internal distinction.

items.b: The search space may exclude the true process.
items.html: If an important role or tool type is missing from the search space, the best recovered workflow can only be an approximation.

items.b: Pruning can remove a late-blooming branch.
items.html: A branch may look weak at shallow depth and then improve after one extra step, so early pruning can discard a candidate that would have become strong because the needed evidence had not appeared yet.
The method is useful because it produces a workflow that humans can edit, compare, and simplify instead of only a hidden model score.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create a hidden reference workflow with a few roles and tool calls, then expose only its task inputs and outputs. Run AgentXRay on those examples and let it search for a stand-in workflow under a fixed budget. After reconstruction, compare the recovered workflow against the reference on both output match and step count.

The demo should show that pruning helps recover a readable workflow with fewer trials because weak branches stop consuming the budget. Show the recovered chain to a human so that the result can be inspected directly.
demo.metric_eq: reconstruction_gain = proxy_match_agentxray - proxy_match_unpruned ; cost_drop = tokens_unpruned - tokens_agentxray
demo.closing: The value of the demo is that a hidden agent becomes a readable editable process.
